asDecan.p: Astrologers cut every sign into three ten-degree slices called decans, and each slice gets a planet of its own and a small card to go with it. Your Sun is somewhere between 10 and 19 degrees of Leo, the middle slice, where the sign has settled in and is running at full strength. In the Golden Dawn order that slice goes to Jupiter. Jupiter has no special dignity in Leo. It's a visitor there, neither helped nor held back, and it takes its colour from the Sun, which rules the sign. So you get Leo's warmth with Jupiter's appetite for more of it, more people, more room, a bigger table. The slice before yours is Saturn and the Five of Wands, which has to fight for its place. The one after is Mars and the Seven, defending the ground once it's been won. Yours sits between them, and it's the one with the parade. Strength is your Sun card overall, and the Six of Wands is the finer grain inside it.

You tend to assume people are pleased to see you, and most of the time you're right, which only makes the habit stronger. You walk into a friend's fortieth and within ten minutes you've introduced two people who've never met and started a toast nobody asked for. In a team meeting you're the one who says out loud that Priya's numbers were the reason the quarter went well, and you mean it, though you also quite like being the person who said it. When a group chat goes quiet after you've shared good news, a new job, the house you finally bought, you notice, and you'll check it again before bed. Sundays with nothing planned don't sit well with you. By eleven you've rung three people and there's a barbecue at yours, and you've bought enough sausages for twenty.

The gift nobody mentions is what you're like when things are going badly. Anyone can lead a victory lap. You're unusually good at the half-time talk when the team is down by twenty, or the Monday after the big client walked, when everyone's staring at their screens and you're the one who books a table for lunch and gets people talking about what's next. It isn't forced cheer, or not usually. Jupiter in you genuinely believes there's more good coming, and people can hear that you believe it. I've seen this in a lot of middle-decan Leos. They're the ones a small business keeps on through a rough year, partly for the work they do and mostly because the place feels less grim when they're in it. You also remember to say well done to the junior who fixed the printer.

Jupiter's weakness is scale, and in Leo it shows up as promising more than a fortnight can hold. You say yes to hosting Christmas, running the school fundraiser and helping your sister move, all in the same stretch, because each one sounded lovely in the moment and you liked being the person who'd do it. Then something gives, usually the least visible thing, which tends to be your own sleep or the friend you said you'd ring. Generosity runs up a bill too. The round of drinks, the extravagant present, the dinner you insisted on paying for, and a card statement you'd rather not open. There's a quieter one as well. When a close friend gets the promotion you'd both gone for, you're first with the champagne, loud and genuinely glad, and then oddly flat for a week, and you don't tell anyone why.

When something goes wrong, your first move is to make it look smaller in public. The business loses its biggest contract, and by that evening you've told everyone it's fine, you've got three leads, it's probably a blessing. Some of that is real Jupiter optimism and some of it is pride that doesn't want the crowd to see a stumble. About a week later the bravado runs out, and it usually runs out at home, where you go quiet and short with the people who never got the upbeat version. They end up feeling shut out of the bad news, which to be honest they have been. Grief can go the same way. You organise the funeral beautifully and fall apart months later over something small. What actually helps is one person you tell the real numbers to early, and permission to cancel the thing you'd promised to host.

You're a proud partner, and it shows. You'll tell a table of strangers how clever your partner is, post the photo from their graduation, turn up to their work do and charm their boss. Most people like being loved out loud, and plenty of them have never had it before you. Where it snags is that you tend to love in the big gestures, the surprise weekend away, the party, and you can be a bit hopeless at the small daily ones, like remembering they hate coriander or noticing they've been tired for a fortnight. Some partners need the second kind much more. There's also the question of who gets the attention in the couple. You're usually the louder one, and it's worth checking every so often that your partner's news gets as much airtime at dinner as yours does.

At work you do well wherever results are public and people are counted on to show up. Sales, teaching, hospitality, events, running a team, any job with a stage in it somewhere, even if the stage is a Monday stand-up. Jupiter in Leo has a knack for being the face of something, and organisations work that out about you quickly and send you to the conference or put you in front of the client. You're generous with credit, which makes people want to work for you. Where you need a system is follow-through on the promises you made while the room was warm. Write down every yes you give in a meeting before you leave the building. And be careful with work that has no audience at all, long solo research or a remote role with nobody to talk to, because you tend to do worse there than your ability would suggest.

At twenty this decan is often the one everyone knows, with the party, the captain's armband, a lot of friends and a lot of plans, and not much sense yet of which of them matter. The applause comes easily at that age and it's hard to tell the real friends from the audience. By the mid-thirties most people with a Sun here have had at least one public setback, a venture that didn't take off, a role they were passed over for, and the ones who come through it tend to get steadier and choosier, with fewer and better commitments. The fifties often bring the Jupiter side forward. Mentoring, sponsoring, handing the wreath to someone else, and a real pleasure in watching a person they backed at thirty end up running the place. The pride is still there, of course.

Once a month, pick one person whose work nobody has noticed, a colleague, the neighbour who mows the verge, your mum, and tell them specifically what they did well, in front of someone else if you can. Then, in the same week, do one thing that matters to you and tell nobody about it. Finish the chapter, run the distance, clear out the shed, and keep it to yourself for at least a fortnight. Notice which of the two was harder.
